## TL;DR

Recorded the server-served mobile web direction in ADR 0011, clarified that it supersedes only the connected-server shell and screen compositions in the mobile UX strategy, and kept the Capacitor picker, lock screen, and isolated WebView architecture valid. Captured the current UI at phone and tablet sizes and filed five ordered follow-up task specifications. No application code or runtime behavior changed.

## Work and rationale

I read the task, the mobile UX strategy, the mobile architecture document, and the UI/preview conventions before editing. Nick clarified that the native apps remain a Capacitor host for many RepoOS servers: the host presents a picker and lock screen, then opens each server's own web UI inside an isolated WebView. The desired change is within that connected server. I revised the ADR to keep the host responsibilities and security model intact while having the server-served SPA render its own narrow-screen composition.

The ADR chooses a 720 CSS pixel boundary. A viewport-based layout composable avoids classifying touch-capable laptops as phones and makes the tablet decision explicit: at 768 pixels, keep the desktop composition and its existing tablet adaptations. This one server-served UI must work in a plain phone browser, the Capacitor host's isolated WebView, and an installed home-screen web app. Navigation, data stores, authentication, and task mutations remain part of the SPA; the Capacitor host remains responsible for choosing and isolating servers. The mobile UX strategy now marks only its connected-server shell and screen composition as superseded. The mobile architecture document is restored unchanged.

I used `repoos shot` on the app target for Work, the task drawer, Settings, Releases, and the dashboard Live activity feed at 390×844 and 768×1024. Activity is represented by the dashboard feed because the router does not expose a separate Activity page. The ADR describes concrete design risks for each surface and does not claim every risk was visually present at both dimensions. These include compressed multi-column Work, a task drawer competing with the board, dense Settings controls, crowded release actions, and an activity feed sharing its page with other dashboard panels.

I filed five follow-up specs through `repoos new` and completed their sections and dependency metadata through `repoos update`: mobile web navigation (#1112), Work queue (#1113), task detail (#1114), Settings (#1115), and cross-surface touch affordances (#1116). The shell task now explicitly says it builds navigation inside the web app and preserves the Capacitor picker, lock screen, and WebView isolation. The dependency order is shell, Work, task detail, Settings after shell, then cross-surface touch fixes. Each task specifies responsive behavior, shared state, touch use, and desktop preservation. No follow-up implementation was started here.

The ADR recommendations now keep #0300's native testing role for the picker, lock screen, WebView isolation, and platform lifecycle, while suggesting browser coverage of the shared narrow UI. It recommends rewriting or closing #0302 to remove a duplicate native connected-server shell, rewriting or closing #0303 depending on how much its Work/detail scope the new tasks replace, and rewriting or closing #0304 while retaining any host-session requirements still needed. The Capacitor picker and isolation responsibilities remain. #1069 is already done; the touch follow-up asks later work to verify its scoped behavior rather than reopen it by default.

## Approaches tried

I initially started multiple `repoos shot` captures concurrently. They queued for the single Playwright slot, but some command calls exceeded their short invocation window. I then ran the remaining captures serially; all ten requested screen/viewport combinations completed. I explicitly selected the app target after the first command showed area-based target resolution selecting the Docs site.

I first created concise follow-up bodies, then RepoOS reported that the task specs lacked standard sections. I revised each to include Problem, Desired UX, Acceptance criteria, and Notes for AI, and corrected dependencies through RepoOS. When Nick's correction arrived, I read it before continuing, revised the ADR and docs, changed #1110's Problem, Desired UX and acceptance criteria through `repoos update`, and clarified #1112's scope through RepoOS as well.

## Challenges and blockers

RepoOS reports that commands from this linked worktree read the canonical board in the main checkout. I used RepoOS commands for task creation and metadata and did not directly inspect or edit that checkout. The create commands warned that their task-file checkpoint could not be committed because the Git identity is unconfigured; later RepoOS updates reported success. I left task metadata to RepoOS's supported workflow rather than attempting direct file edits.

The Activity surface is a dashboard panel rather than a routed page. I captured `/` at both dimensions and documented the exact surface in the ADR. The screenshots are baseline evidence only; this task made no UI code changes.

## Key learnings

The native host and the server's responsive UI are separate layers. Preserving that boundary keeps multi-server selection and WebView isolation while allowing a single consistent connected-server experience across browser, WebView, and installed web app.

The repo already has useful responsive behavior, so globally deleting narrow CSS would risk desktop and tablet regressions. The ADR retires compression rules alongside each replacement composition. The task graph puts shared web navigation first, feature compositions next, and cross-surface touch cleanup after the relevant screens exist. Finally, #1069 shows why touch behavior should remain scoped to its trigger; follow-up work should preserve its tested pointer-cancellation and click behavior instead of introducing a global gesture layer.
